segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pursue love, and be eager for the spiritual gifts, but even more that you may prophesy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to people but to God; for no one understands, but in the Spirit such a person speaks mysteries.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who prophesies speaks to people for building up and encouragement and comfort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever speaks in a tongue builds themselves up, but whoever prophesies builds up the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more that you may prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless that person interprets, so that the assembly may receive building up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now, brothers and sisters, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you by revelation or by knowledge or by prophecy or by teaching?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even with lifeless things that give a sound, whether pipe or lyre: if they give no distinction to the notes, how will it be known what is being played on the pipe or the lyre?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And indeed, if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will get ready for battle?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also with you: if with the tongue you do not give intelligible speech, how will it be known what is being said? For you will be speaking into the air.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are, it may be, so many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without meaning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the one speaking, and the one speaking a foreigner to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also with you: since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, seek to abound for the building up of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue should pray to be able to interpret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? I will pray with my spirit, and I will pray with my mind also; I will sing with my spirit, and I will sing with my mind also.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say the Amen to your thanksgiving, since that person does not know what you are saying?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you are giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not built up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my mind, so that I may instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, do not be children in your thinking; in evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the Law it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “By people of other tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they listen to me, says the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, tongues are for a sign not to those who believe but to unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if the whole assembly comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in, that person is convicted by all, examined by all,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the secrets of their heart come to light, and so, falling facedown, they will worship God, declaring,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God is truly among you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then, brothers and sisters? When you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let everything be done for building up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be two or at most three, and one at a time, and let one person interpret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if there is no interpreter, let each of them keep silent in the assembly and speak to themselves and to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if a revelation comes to another who is seated, let the first keep silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for God is not a God of disorder but of peace), as in all the assemblies of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the women keep silent in the assemblies, for they are not permitted to speak; rather, let them be subject, as the Law also says.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If they want to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or was it from you that the word of God went out? Or are you the only ones it has reached?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone thinks they are a prophet or a spiritual person, they should recognize that what I am writing to you is the Lord's.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone does not recognize this, they are not recognized.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but let everything be done decently and in order.

notes.note: The Greek word means both the tongue as an organ and a language, and Paul plays on both senses (see verse 9). ‘Tongue’ is kept because English can still carry both. Whether Paul has in mind human languages unknown to the speaker or speech of no human kind is debated; the chapter assumes only that hearers cannot understand it without interpretation.

notes.traditional: in the Spirit / in his spirit
notes.note: The Greek has simply ‘in spirit’, without an article, and could mean God's Spirit or the speaker's own spirit, as in verses 14–16, where Paul sets ‘my spirit’ against ‘my mind’. Translations are divided. The reference to God's Spirit is chosen here because Paul has just described tongues as a gift the Spirit gives (12:10), but the other reading is equally possible.

The traditional rendering is ‘church’, which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas ‘church’ now suggests a building or an institution. In this chapter the sense of people actually gathered in one place is especially prominent.

Many translations have ‘flute’ and ‘harp’. The aulos was a reed-blown pipe, closer to an oboe than to a modern flute, and the kithara was a large lyre rather than a harp. They were the standard wind and string instruments of Greek public life.

The Greek says literally that the Corinthians are ‘eager for spirits’. Most interpreters take this as shorthand for the Spirit's gifts or workings, and the rendering follows that view because ‘spirits’ alone would mislead. A minority think Paul is echoing the Corinthians' own way of speaking about inspiring spirits. The same plural recurs in verse 32, ‘the spirits of prophets’.

The word denotes a layperson or non-expert, someone without the relevant training or skill (compare Acts 4:13; 2 Corinthians 11:6). Here it may mean any worshipper who does not understand the tongue being spoken, or a distinct group of interested outsiders who are not yet full members; verses 23–24 set such people alongside unbelievers. Translations vary among ‘outsider’, ‘inquirer’, ‘unlearned’ and ‘ungifted’.

‘The Law’ here means Scripture as a whole, not only the five books of Moses. The quotation is from Isaiah 28:11–12, where God warns that Israel, having refused plain speech, will hear him through the foreign language of invaders. Paul's wording matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint closely.

The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which many translations keep; others use ‘God's people’. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel.

notes.phrase: as in all the assemblies of the holy ones
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had little or no punctuation, and this clause can close the preceding sentence, as here and in the SBLGNT, or open the next: ‘As in all the assemblies of the holy ones, let the women keep silent.’ Many modern translations take the second option. The first avoids the awkward repetition ‘in all the assemblies ... in the assemblies’, though it leaves the clause trailing loosely after the parenthesis.

notes.phrase: Let the women keep silent in the assemblies
notes.note: A few manuscripts of the Western tradition place verses 34–35 after verse 40. Some scholars conclude from this that the two verses began as a marginal comment and are not Paul's; others point out that no surviving manuscript omits them. The SBLGNT prints them here without brackets.

The Greek word means both ‘women’ and ‘wives’, and verse 35 (‘their own husbands’) suggests that married women are in view. Since Paul assumes in 11:5 that women pray and prophesy in the gathering, most interpreters take the silence required here to be limited in some way rather than absolute, though how is disputed. Which passage of ‘the Law’ is meant is also uncertain; Genesis 3:16 is often suggested.

notes.traditional: is a command of the Lord
notes.note: The SBLGNT reads simply ‘is the Lord's’. Most manuscripts, and most translations, read ‘is a command of the Lord’ or ‘are commands of the Lord’. The shorter reading has limited manuscript support, but the variation among the longer forms suggests that the word was added to complete the sense.

notes.traditional: let him be ignorant / he is not recognized
notes.note: Paul echoes verse 37: whoever does not recognize this is not recognized, probably by God, possibly by the community. Many later manuscripts have an imperative instead, ‘let him be ignorant’, which the King James Version follows. The verb can also mean ‘ignore’, giving ‘if anyone ignores this, he is ignored’.

candidates.reason: Recurs in Acts and 1 Corinthians 12–14, where ‘tongue’ and ‘language’ are both defensible, and the choice needs to be uniform for the gift of speech.
The plural address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters, and translators divide between ‘brothers’ and ‘brothers and sisters’.
‘Mystery’ in English suggests a puzzle, whereas the Greek usually means a secret now disclosed; it recurs across Paul, the Gospels and Revelation.
With its verb οἰκοδομέω it recurs across Paul; ‘edification/edify’ and ‘building up/build up’ compete, and the construction metaphor should be handled consistently.
The substantive use recurs in 1 Corinthians 2, 12 and 14 and elsewhere, and whether to supply ‘gifts’, ‘things’ or ‘people’ needs one policy.
